feedback: If the rule drifts mid-sort (starts by colour, slips to size or 'ones I like'), pause and have the child say their ONE rule aloud and hold it up, then re-run the sort against that fixed rule — the idea is fine, the procedure just needs anchoring.

If the child sorts by what objects are FOR ('the cup and jar go together because they hold things'), redirect to 'what is it MADE of / what is it LIKE to touch?'; if it persists, practise describing one material's properties before grouping.

If the child treats each material as having one permanent home and cannot re-sort, make the same object land in different groups in front of them — foil with the wood under 'see-through vs not see-through' (neither is see-through), foil with the fabric and sponge under 'bendy vs stiff' — so the group is seen to follow the chosen property.
Praise naming the rule and justifying placements with property words, not just getting items in the 'right' pile.
activities.intendedInsight: A group is not a fixed fact about an object; it depends on the property you choose to look at. The same material can belong with different partners under different rules.
learnerActions: Lay out a tray of real materials: wood block, glass jar, metal key, plastic toy, sponge, foil, fabric.
Choose ONE property and say the rule out loud before touching anything (e.g. 'see-through vs not see-through').
Sort every item into two hoops or trays, saying a property word for each placement ('I put the glass jar with the clear plastic toy because you can see through both').
Now sort the SAME items again, but pick a DIFFERENT property (e.g. bendy vs stiff, or hard vs softer). Notice which items move home.

Point out an item that changed groups and say why (e.g. 'the foil was with the wood for not see-through, but with the fabric and sponge for bendy'; the glass only leaves the plastic under 'hard' if the plastic toy is soft or squashy).

If you are ready, use two overlapping hoops labelled with two different properties (e.g. 'shiny' and 'hard') and put an item that has both, such as the metal key, in the overlap; an either/or pair like see-through vs not see-through or bendy vs stiff has no true overlap.
activities.title: Sort real materials, then re-sort by a new rule

feedback: If the child names a use or feeling ('I like it') instead of a property, ask 'what is it like — hard or soft? shiny or dull? see-through or not?'
Accept any defensible property as long as it is a property of the material, and check the 'same' and 'different' entries actually match the two items.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing two materials by naming a shared and a differing property is the bridge from describing one material to grouping many.
learnerActions: Take just two materials at a time (e.g. glass jar and clear plastic toy; or wood block and metal key).
Say one property they SHARE ('both are hard' or 'you can see through both').
Say one property where they DIFFER ('the glass is see-through but the wood is not').
Record each in a 'same' column and a 'different' column, using property words.
Repeat with other pairs so comparing becomes a stepping stone into sorting a larger jumble.
activities.title: Same-and-different pair comparison
